vignette:
Michael

Michael sits with his hands clasped tightly in his lap, his callused fingers bearing the familiar marks of twenty years spent with tools. At thirty, he looks older than his years-there's a weariness in his shoulders, a tension that seems permanently etched into his jaw. He's been married to Sarah for four years, and they recently bought a house together, a modest Victorian that he's been restoring on weekends. Or trying to, anyway.

The accident happened two years ago on a Tuesday in March. Michael was framing the second floor of a residential addition when his coworker and friend, Danny, fell from the scaffolding. It was only twelve feet-not the kind of fall that should have been fatal. But Danny landed on a concrete pad in exactly the wrong way, and Michael watched his body go still. He remembers the sound more than anything else: a wet, heavy thud that doesn't match anything in his previous experience. He remembers climbing down the ladder with shaking hands, remembers kneeling beside Danny while someone called 911, remembers the strange angle of Danny's neck.

Danny died three days later without regaining consciousness.

For months afterward, Michael continued working. He had to-they needed the income, and he didn't know what else to do with himself. But something had shifted fundamentally. He became hypervigilant on job sites, constantly scanning for hazards, mentally calculating worst-case scenarios for every task. His supervisor noticed he was slower, more cautious, double-checking safety equipment obsessively. A job that should have taken three weeks stretched to five. Other carpenters started avoiding him, sensing something off in his demeanor.

The nightmares began around four months post-accident. Michael would wake at three or four in the morning, his shirt drenched with sweat, his heart hammering. The dreams weren't always about the fall itself-sometimes he was falling, sometimes he was watching it happen again and again, sometimes Danny's face morphed into the faces of his other coworkers. Sarah would find him downstairs at two in the morning, sitting in the dark kitchen, unable to articulate why he couldn't sleep.

Now, two years later, Michael has pulled back significantly from carpentry. He still works, but he's taken on mostly solo renovation projects and smaller jobs where he can control the environment. He avoids heights when possible, which is increasingly difficult in his line of work. He's turned down lucrative contracts because the thought of being on a multi-story scaffold makes his chest tight and his breathing shallow. Just last week, a potential client asked him to bid on a commercial project, and Michael felt such acute dread that he invented an excuse rather than visit the site.

His marriage has strained under the weight of it all. Sarah tries to be understanding, but Michael has become withdrawn. He snaps at her over small things-a loud noise, an unexpected touch, her mentioning that she's going rock climbing with friends. He's stopped attending social gatherings with the crew. He doesn't talk about Danny anymore, though Sarah knows he thinks about him constantly. Sometimes she finds Michael staring out the window for hours, his expression distant and haunted.

The house renovation sits half-finished. Michael can't bring himself to work on the second-floor bedroom. He starts projects and abandons them. He's gained weight from inactivity and stress, and he feels the loss of his former identity as a capable, confident tradesman. The work that once gave him pride now feels like a minefield, and he's not sure how much longer he can sustain this version of himself.
